metadata.description: TPM 2.0 Sealing Configuration for ShadowCypher Enterprise

tpm_device.documentation: Standard Linux TPM 2.0 character device interface

sealing_policy.name: ShadowCypher_Primary_Sealing
sealing_policy.description: Seals encryption keys to platform firmware, configuration, and secure boot state

pcr0.name: Core Root of Trust for Measurement
pcr0.purpose: Detects firmware modifications or malicious BIOS

pcr1.name: Platform Configuration
pcr1.purpose: Detects hardware changes or hardware swaps
pcr1.stability: Changes only on significant hardware modifications
pcr1.risk_high_reason: Minor hardware changes (RAM upgrade) may trigger re-sealing

pcr7.name: Secure Boot State
pcr7.binds_to: Secure Boot enablement, Boot Manager, Bootloader
pcr7.purpose: Detects secure boot bypass or tampering
pcr7.risk_high_reason: Disabling secure boot prevents unsealing - requires recovery key

sealing_workflow: 2. Create sealing policy: keys only unseal when PCRs match
3. Seal encryption key with TPM primary key
4. Store sealed blob (cannot be read without matching PCRs)

key_derivation.documentation: Master key never leaves TPM; backup key provides independent access

backup_unsealing.purpose: Recovery access if TPM fails or is inaccessible
backup_unsealing.security_model: Separate security boundary from TPM; requires secure storage
recommendations: Store backup key in password manager (KeePass, 1Password, Bitwarden)
Keep copy in physical safe or secure location
Rotate annually or after security incidents
Audit all backup key usage attempts

scenario_1.name: TPM Hardware Failure
steps: Proceed with system recovery or replacement

scenario_2.name: Firmware Update (PCR Change)
steps: Run: tpm2-config.sh seal-create (creates new sealing policy)
Generate new backup key: tpm2-config.sh backup-key-generate

scenario_3.name: Secure Boot Disabled
scenario_3.action: Recovery access and re-enable secure boot
steps: Boot from recovery media (may not have TPM-sealed access)
Re-seal keys: tpm2-config.sh seal-create && tpm2-config.sh seal-key

assumptions: TPM 2.0 module is genuine and firmware is not compromised
Secure Boot is enabled and enforced throughout boot chain
Physical access to device is controlled
System entropy is sufficient for cryptographic operations
Backup key is stored securely (separate from device)

protected_against.encryption_key_extraction: Key sealed in TPM, never plaintext on disk
protected_against.secure_boot_bypass: PCR7 sealing detects boot integrity violations
protected_against.unauthorized_unsealing: Requires matching PCRs or backup key

not_protected_against: Physical attacks on TPM module (side-channel, reverse engineering)
Compromised kernel post-boot (integrity assumes clean boot)
Cold-boot attacks (mitigated by FDE + RAM encryption, not TPM)
Hypervisor attacks in VM environments (requires vTPM + different model)

security_controls: SC-7: Cryptographic binding to hardware platform
SC-28: Encrypted key material at rest

initial_setup.description: Steps to set up TPM 2.0 sealing for the first time

procedures.description: Verify TPM 2.0 is present and accessible
Initialize TPM environment and create primary key
Create sealing policy based on current PCR values
Seal the LUKS master key to TPM

procedures.important: Store backup key in secure location, separate from device

maintenance.daily: Monitor system for TPM errors in logs
maintenance.quarterly: Test recovery procedures with backup key
maintenance.annually: Update firmware, rotate backup key, re-seal keys
